entries.title: Three men shot in South Lawndale, two hours after another man shot blocks away
entries.summary: <p>Three people were shot blocks from the Cook County Criminal Courthouse Tuesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Someone inside a tan sedan fired shots, striking three men in the 2400 block of South Washtenaw Avenue at 8:44 p.m., police said.</p><p>A 21-year-old was shot in the head and taken to Stroger Hospital in serious condition, police said. A 27-year-old man was shot in the head and listed in critical condition, and a 22-year-old was shot in the leg and was listed in good condition; both were taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital.</p><p>About two hours earlier, another man was shot in the 2700 block of West 25th Street at 6:33 p.m. while standing in front of a home, police said. He was taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital in good condition.</p><p>No one is in custody related to either shooting, police said.</p>

entries.title: CBS' '60 minutes' announces new slate of correspondents for upcoming season
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — Two months after a major shakeup, CBS’s “60 Minutes” has hired a lineup of new correspondents and contributors in time for its 59th season, including Ross Douthat, a conservative opinion columnist at The New York Times, and Norah O'Donnell, former anchor of “CBS Evening News.”</p><p>The show's new executive producer, Nick Bilton, announced the news in a staff memo Tuesday, shared on X. Joining Douthat and O'Donnell will be author Sebastian Junger, Trevor Phillips and Gianna Toboni. All will be contributors to the show.</p><p>The new journalists join current correspondents Lesley Stahl, Jon Wertheim and Bill Whitaker. Their hirings come two months after a shakeup at the storied program, led by the network's new editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss.</p><p>Weiss installed Bilton, who has little substantive broadcast news experience, as executive producer, replacing Tanya Simon, who was let go after a 30-plus year tenure with the show. Also let go were correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega — and soon after, Scott Pelley, after a tense confrontation with his bosses over the changes.</p><p>In addition to the three dismissed, Anderson Cooper — whose primary job is at CNN — said earlier this year he was leaving of his own accord after two decades.</p><h3>CBS News leaders enthused about the hires</h3><p>Weiss and Tom Cibrowski, the CBS News president, praised the new hires in an internal memo. “We couldn’t be more excited about this news,” the two said, welcoming the new additions. “Onward!”</p><p>Bilton called Douthat “one of the preeminent public intellectuals in America today, a thinker of uncommon rigor and a journalist of deep empathy.” The columnist has spent nearly two decades at the Times and is an author of numerous books.</p><p>The producer called O’Donnell “a powerhouse.”</p><p>“You’ve seen her all over the network. She’s launched a new podcast. And you’ll see much more of her in our halls because Norah will be a correspondent on 60 Minutes."</p><p>Bilton praised Junger for his nonfiction work “The Perfect Storm,” about a catastrophic 1991 storm. The book “landed with an electric charge in the world of reported nonfiction, defining an intense and intimate form of storytelling and establishing Sebastian as a generational talent,” Bilton said.</p><p>Toboni joins “60 Minutes” as a contributor and CBS News as a national correspondent. Previously a senior correspondent with VICE News and VICE on HBO, she comes to the program from CNN.</p><p>Calling her a journalist of “extraordinary range,” Bilton noted that Toboni has interviewed members of ISIS, investigated cartel violence in Mexico and has written a book on the death penalty.</p><p>Also serving as contributor will be Trevor Phillips, announced last month as the news division's senior global affairs correspondent. Based in London, he is “one of the most respected and trusted voices in the United Kingdom for his ability to ask the toughest questions and hold anyone in power to account,” Bilton wrote in his memo.</p><h3>‘60 Minutes’ has faced upheaval for a while</h3><p>Turmoil had raged at “60 Minutes” for more than a year before the May shakeup. Much of it came after President Donald Trump sued the show over its editing of a 2024 interview with then-Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.</p><p>That became part of a broader shakeup at CBS News after Weiss was named to the new role of editor-in-chief by parent company Paramount late last year following David Ellison’s arrival as the network’s corporate leader.</p>

entries.title: Bomb threat cleared at Evanston hospital
entries.summary: <p>Police gave the all clear Tuesday after a suspicious package found outside Endeavor Health Evanston Hospital prompted the building to be locked down for a bomb threat investigation.</p><p>Officials closed the hospital around 5:30 p.m. and deployed a drone to survey the “suspicious package with wires protruding from it," Evanston police said in a statement. The Cook County Bomb Squad was also on the scene.</p><p>The area around the hospital was reopened around 8:10 p.m. after the package was determined not to be a threat, police said.</p>

entries.title: 4 tornadoes hit Chicago area during Monday's storms, officials say
entries.summary: <p>People across the greater Chicago area on Tuesday were dealing with the effects of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" target="_blank" >heavy thunderstorms</a> and four confirmed tornadoes from the day before.</p><p>A clear, sunny day brought some relief, as floodwaters receded, basements could at least start to dry out, damages were assessed and power was being restored across the region.</p><p>Officials said the communities hit hardest during Monday’s storm include Chicago Heights, Maywood, Crestwood, Bolingbrook, University Park, Libertyville and portions of the South Side.</p><p>The four tornadoes touched down in the south and west suburbs, survey teams with the National Weather Service confirmed Tuesday afternoon and evening. </p><p>One tornado hit south suburban Lansing, while another passed through south suburban Country Club Hills, Hazel Crest, Harvey and Homewood. Both tornadoes had gusts topping 110 mph, according to the weather service.</p><p>The other two tornadoes hit west suburban Glen Ellyn and south suburban Orland Park, each with winds reaching a max of 85 mph, according to the weather service.</p><p>Big wind gusts were recorded elsewhere across the city and suburbs, topping out at 82 mph recorded in Waukegan, according to the weather service. Midway Airport recorded winds of 73 mph, and O’Hare Airport saw 65 mph winds.</p><p>The weather service said it also confirmed damaging straight line winds in Carol Stream and Downers Grove, and that surveyors would continue to assess the damage across the region.</p><p>Besides the damaging wind, the downpour flooded hundreds of basements.</p><p>Chicago reported at least 599 flooded homes, according to the city’s Office of Emergency Management and Communications. Among Chicago’s wards, the one with the most reports of flooded basements was the 8th Ward on the Far South Side.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-750000" name="html-embed-module-750000"></a><div style="min-height:918px" id="datawrapper-vis-SXryo"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SXryo/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-SXryo"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SXryo/full.png" alt="Across the city, Chicagoans called in thousands of times to 311 due to yesterday's storms (Choropleth map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In some pockets of Cook County those 2 inches of rain fell in just two hours, according to the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District.</p><p>The heavy rain overwhelmed some streets and drainage systems. Chicago’s official climate station at O’Hare measured 1.76 inches, while Midway received 2.94 inches. Much of the Chicago area saw 2 to 4 inches of rain.</p><p>The two major reservoirs managing that rainfall both are filling, with one nearing capacity <a class="Link" href="https://mwrd.org/" target="_blank" >according to the MWRD</a>, with McCook Reservoir about 93% full, storing about 4.8 billion gallons. The Thornton Reservoir, to the south, is about 42% full, storing nearly 3.6 billion gallons.</p><p>In Downers Grove, meanwhile, crews on Tuesday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/28/downers-grove-sewer-storm-drain" target="_blank" >recovered the body</a> of a contractor trapped in a Downers Grove storm drain during the storm.</p><p>Besides all those flooded basements, Chicago also reported receiving 2,322 calls about trees that were down or damaged, and 973 reports of tree debris. Add that to the roughly 40,000 requests for service involving downed or damaged trees, or tree debris, the city received from June 10 through July 7, when several intense storms hit the city.</p><p>Chicago officials also said the recent storm led to 623 reports of water on streets and 47 flooded viaducts around Chicago as well as 310 traffic signals out; 220 streetlights out; 160 downed wires; and 116 damaged streetlight poles as of Tuesday afternoon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7e0000" name="html-embed-module-7e0000"></a><div style="min-height:606px" id="datawrapper-vis-pDMHz"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/pDMHz/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-pDMHz"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/pDMHz/full.png" alt="As yesterday's storm rolled in, Chicagoans placed thousands of calls to the city's 311 hotline (Area Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>According to ComEd, more than 530,000 customers lost power as a result of the storm. By Tuesday morning, crews had restored electricity to nearly 300,000 customers, according to ComEd. The utility expects that by noon Wednesday it will have restored power to about 80% of those who lost their electricity. The rest of ComEd customers will have power restored by 10 p.m. Friday, according to the utility.</p><p>In south suburban Crete, Kristin Webster said she heard wind and rain whipping through her neighborhood Monday afternoon. By the time the storm passed, much of the village lost power, and for Webster, it still hasn’t been restored. </p><p>Webster, 46, observed several downed trees in the area, including two that crushed her neighbors’ cars. But the most frustrating part of dealing with the storm’s aftermath has been how long it’s been since the initial damage.</p><p>“Nobody should be put in the situation where they can't have the normal comforts of home, especially 30 hours later,” she told the Chicago Sun-Times. “I've never seen anything like this.”</p><p>Webster said she anticipates throwing away refrigerated food that will go bad before power is restored, and she plans to drive 40 minutes south to a friend’s home that has power in order to refrigerate some medication.</p><p>In a post on social media, ComEd acknowledged the frustration people without power are facing, but said the severe weather is nearly unprecedented, and it will take time to restore power to everyone.</p><p>“When storms cause this level of damage across dozens of communities at the same time, restoration becomes significantly more complex,” the post reads.</p><p></p><p>Additionally, AT&T has reported wireless disruptions primarily within Cook and DuPage counties. An AT&T spokesperson said “we are working as quickly and safely as possible to restore service.”</p><p>The Illinois American Red Cross has also opened two shelters, in Steger and Gurnee, to help those affected by the storm. According to regional communications director Connie Esparza, many Illinoisans have come to the shelter for access to electricity and food, with some staying overnight.</p><p>As cleanup efforts continue, officials are urging residents to avoid downed power lines, report hazards and use caution while traveling through areas still affected by flooding, fallen trees and power outages.</p>

entries.title: Is injured White Sox catcher Kyle Teel catching with a walking boot?
entries.summary: <p>As reporters sat in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> dugout waiting for manager Will Venable to speak Tuesday, injured catcher Kyle Teel emerged from the tunnel connected to the clubhouse dressed in full gear: mask, chest protector and shin guards. He was only eight days removed from suffering a high sprain of his left ankle and had been seen wearing a walking boot the night before.</p><p>Was this a miraculous recovery from an injury that’s expected to shelve Teel for six to 12 weeks?</p><p>As it turned out, no, it wasn’t. As Teel walked past the assembled media, his walking boot became visible after being hidden by the shin guard. But it was a sight not seen before. Oblivious to the watchful eyes, Teel walked through the dugout and headed to the bullpen, where he caught light baseballs while seated or kneeling in an effort to stay sharp.</p><p>“I wasn’t aware that was part of the plan today,” Venable said. “If [trainer James Kruk] is OK with it, I’m sure it’s fine.”</p><p>Venable said that nothing has changed regarding Teel’s timetable and that he hasn’t done any baseball activities since the injury — at least until Tuesday.</p><p>“That’s the first,” Venable said. “He’s been really stationary to this point.”</p><p>It’s evidence of Teel’s work ethic and perhaps his FOMO (fear of missing out, for those unfamiliar with the acronym). But the Sox don’t want him pushing his limits.</p><p>“There’s always that back and forth between the player and the training staff,” Venable said. “Really a collaboration in trying to figure out what’s the right amount to push or when and how to go about it. Unfortunately with these injuries, he’s learning how to go about his treatment and handle it the right way.</p><p>“No update other than Kyle is going about this with a really positive attitude and doing a great job of getting his work in. And obviously with a boot on, still finding ways to get work in and get his treatment in, as well.”</p><h3>Maddon’s influence</h3><p>Venable learned a lot as a base coach under former Cubs manager Joe Maddon from 2018 to 2020. One of those lessons was to have few team meetings. But as the Sox’ manager, Venable has put his own spin on it, hosting what he calls “state of the Sox” meetings monthly.</p><p>“I address the team, and we just open the floor to talk about things,” Venable said. “That’s the time where if there are broader issues to discuss, we’ll talk about those things.</p><p>“Joe Maddon would meet with the team three times a year; would never ever do other kinds of meetings. There’s something about that that I liked. Not rigid about it, but just want to have a routine that they know we’re going to get together and talk.”</p><p>One topic at the next meeting might be the trade deadline, which is at 5 p.m. Monday. That can be a distraction for everyone and could be worth discussing.</p><p>“Rarely do the players have stuff. It happens every once in a while,” Venable said. “It’s in the spirit of being proactive and not having a team meeting in response to a thing and just creating a platform for guys if they have something. They haven’t been that heavy, to be honest.”</p><h3>Challenging challenges</h3><p>When the Sox used — and lost — both of their pitch challenges in the first inning Sunday, Steve Stone offered biting analysis on the Chicago Sports Network broadcast: “Not a great plan.”</p><p>Indeed not. But Venable doesn’t want the Sox leaving a game with unused challenges. He wants his players to be aggressive with them. How aggressive is still being determined.</p><p>“It’s been real challenging to find the right tone and guidelines to put in place,” Venable said. “You want to support and empower them to use this as a tool that can help swing an at-bat, can swing a game. And at the same time, there’s times where it’s not great to challenge if you’re not sure.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: American Airlines flights grounded nationwide for tech issue
entries.summary: <p>A “technology issue” grounded American Airlines flights across the country on Tuesday, according to the company.</p><p>It was unclear how many flights at Chicago’s airports were impacted, with average delays sitting around a half hour. A ground stop was temporarily issued by the Federal Aviation Administration just for the airline.</p><p>“Systems are coming back online now and flights are departing again,” the company said on social media. “We apologize to our customers for the inconvenience.”</p><p>At O’Hare Airport, more than 1,000 flights had been canceled in the last 24 hours — with nearly 600 facing more than 45 minutes of delays — while 267 had been canceled. At Midway, 222 flights were delayed, the majority of which being less than half an hour, with 13 total cancellations.<br></p>

entries.title: Crews recover body of second contractor trapped in Downers Grove sewer during storm
entries.summary: <p>The body of a contractor trapped in a Downers Grove storm drain was recovered on Tuesday, a day after two workers went missing as storms moved through the area.</p><p>Crews recovered the body around 5 p.m., town officials said on social media, more than a day after they rescued the other employee from the sewer drain.</p><p>The worker's identity has not been released. The DuPage County coroner’s office was determining the cause and manner of death, town officials said.</p><p>The rescue effort began around 12:50 p.m. Monday, when a Vortex employee flagged down Downers Grove police officers in the 800 block of Curtiss Street, town officials said. The employee told police that two workers were trapped in the storm drains. Downers Grove firefighters later arrived to perform a rescue.</p><p>Two hours later, firefighters rescued one of the workers about 200 feet down the drain, officials said. He was taken to Good Samaritan Hospital in good condition.</p><p>The second worker was found dead Tuesday in the storm sewer near Washington Street, officials said.</p><p>Officials said the man worked for the Houston, Texas-based Vortex Lining Systems LLC. </p><p>"We are devastated by the loss of our team member following an unexpected major rain event, and are doing everything we can to support his family during this incredibly difficult time," the company said in a statement. "We thank rescue crew members and first responders for their tremendous efforts."</p><p>The Occupational Safety and Health Administration was investigating the incident.</p><p>The employees had been working on a large-diameter pipe rehabilitation project to help maintain an 11-foot diameter, 2,200 foot long pipe installed in the 1960s that carries water from the St Joseph Creek to downtown Downers Grove. The project, begun last year, is set to be completed by the end of 2027.</p>

entries.title: Cubs, already strong, eye getting even better at trade deadline: ‘Hopefully we get everything we want’
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — While <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> players lamented <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/27/cubs-jameson-taillon-dfa-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-rotation" >the departure of veteran pitcher <b>Jameson Taillon</b></a> on Monday, they weren’t naive about any supposed blindside.</p><p>They know this sort of thing can happen in this game, particularly when the stakes are as high as they are for this Cubs team.</p><p>In the thick of a playoff race and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >chasing the division-leading Brewers</a> in the NL Central, the Cubs’ championship-level aspirations rest on what happens the next few months.</p><p>That starts with <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s front office getting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/22/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-jed-hoyer-pitching-nico-hoerner-buyers-nl-central-standings-brewers" >a last shot at tweaking the roster</a> at the trade deadline, with the intent of best positioning these Cubs for a deep October run.</p><p>“You remove the personal stuff as much as you can,” second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> said Monday. “It’s always their job to put the best possible team they can on the field.</p><p>“Absolutely, there’s urgency. These games go by fast, and the season gets short. We have a lot of really exciting things ahead of us.”</p><p>Believing in the capability of the position-player group, Hoyer & Co. will be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >fixating on pitching improvements</a> ahead of Monday’s deadline, attempting to strengthen an area of the roster where the depth has been tested by injuries and, in Taillon’s case, underperformance.</p><p>Though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/16/cubs-second-half-preview-brewers-nl-central-standings-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-craig-counsell-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-alex-bregman" >the Cubs have earned justified plaudits</a> for weathering all those injuries and a monthlong slump to own one of the best records in baseball, going from good to great to even better by winning the trade-deadline arms race can be the difference come October.</p><p>“Our group has some pretty special things about it,” Hoerner said. “We’re not perfect, and we’re in a place now where we can definitely make some improvements to a team that’s already really strong.</p><p>“The time leading up to the trade deadline does feel different. It’s exciting. It’s an opportunity.”</p><p>Veterans of their depth being tested this year — and of that depth proving an issue during last year’s briefer-than-hoped playoff stay — the Cubs are simultaneously excited by who they already have and who they might add, the benefits of setting the front office up to buy at this time of year.</p><p>Will Hoyer’s work be enough for the Cubs to catch the Brewers or play deep into October? Time will tell.</p><p>“We want to be in this spot,” third baseman <b>Alex Bregman</b> said. “We want to be contending this time of year and making our team better and better. The guys in this room have done a good job of getting us to where we need to be.</p><p>“Hopefully we get everything we want.”</p><h3><b>Best Happ play ever?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b>’s throw to cut down a runner trying to advance to second on a hit off the wall in the eighth inning Monday deserved its highlight-reel status.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">IAN HAPP IS PUTTING ON A DEFENSIVE CLINIC. <a href="https://t.co/pIgQGYrUB6">pic.twitter.com/pIgQGYrUB6</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2081951916473393456?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 28, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><p>But just how high does it rank on the all-time great-plays list for the four-time Gold Glover?</p><p>“I told Ian that’s the best defensive play I’ve seen him make in the three years I’ve been here,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “I thought it was an incredible play.”</p><p>“We’ve thrown out a lot of guys together on balls down the line,” said Hoerner, who applied the tag at second base, “but off the wall like that is pretty rare and tough to do.”</p><h3><b>Bats are boomin’</b></h3><p>The Cubs’ offense stayed scorching in Tuesday’s 10-2 win over the Cardinals. They’ve scored 35 runs in their last four games, an average of 8.8 runs per contest.</p><p>The Cubs came into Tuesday third in baseball in runs scored, with 548, then added on by double digits.</p><p>“It was pretty relentless,” said left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b>, who doubled twice. “We have so many good players in this lineup that play every day, and I have all the confidence in the world this group is going to put up those kinds of numbers because that’s who we are.”</p><h3><b>Hoerner’s hot</b></h3><h3></h3><p>After collecting five hits in the first two games of the Cubs' series against the Cardinals, Hoerner is batting .417 with 12 RBIs in 11 games since the All-Star break.</p><p>“I’ve hit a good amount of line drives, that’s always a good thing. When I’m at my best, I’m hitting balls all over the field,” Hoerner said. “I’ve gotten some balls to fall that weren’t hit the hardest, which always helps.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel entries.title: Illinois football coach Bret Bielema is bullish on the Big Ten
entries.summary: <p>With Jim Harbaugh long gone to the NFL, the Big Ten Media Days don’t have quite the same edge. When the three-day event kicked off at the Hilton Chicago on Tuesday, there was a lot of inside-football talk about 3-3-5 defenses and plenty of coach-speak about leadership and cohesion.</p><p>But there also was substantive discussion of some of the storm clouds hovering over college sports in general and football in particular. And as usual, there were a few zingers from Illinois coach Bret Bielema.</p><p>He didn’t wait long to take a shot at the SEC, which has been going back-and-forth with the Big Ten about which is the best football conference.</p><p>“They want to live in 2005 forever,” Bielema said.</p><p>He’s qualified to talk about the two leagues, having been a coach in both with stints at Wisconsin and Illinois wrapped around a forgettable stint at Arkansas.</p><p>A follow-up question on his SEC hot take led to Bielema weighing in on the Big Ten’s much-maligned and long-gone division names: Leaders and Legends.</p><p>“I don’t know how the hell we got there,” Bielema said, echoing the feelings of most fans and the rest of the college football world.</p><p>Wondering how he got to talking about the names of almost forgotten divisions? It was part of a story about the need to turn the page, which he clearly believes the SEC should do.</p><p>Bielema recalled his unhappiness about Wisconsin not getting the same respect as some traditional powers when the divisions were created. He vented to longtime Wisconsin coach-turned-athletic director Barry Alvarez, who told him: “Don’t worry about things you can’t control. You can’t change people’s 50 years of history in the way they think.”</p><p>It was another way of saying that was then and this is now. The Big Ten has produced the last three national champions — won by three different schools — meaning the SEC has to come up with another argument for its supposed superiority.</p><p>That argument, which former Alabama coach Nick Saban and others have been peddling lately, boils down to the SEC being a deeper conference.</p><p>Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti pushed back hard against that narrative.</p><p>“The idea that the middle of our conference isn’t hard is just not right,” Petitti said. “At the end of the day, our teams are ready for the CFP. Our travel looks like the CFP travel. You’re going all over the country. The difficulty [of winning] on the road in the Big Ten — I just think that’s overlooked.”</p><p>Which conference plays better football is a fun argument. A more serious discussion is whether and how college sports can remain sustainable as more and more money pours into some programs and not to others.</p><p>“I don’t think you’ll talk to an AD or even a coach or anybody in the country that will tell you that exponential growth, every portal, is the right model,” Petitti said.</p><p>“We need to get to a place where we can have a model of growth that’s more realistic and looks more like what our revenue growth could possibly be.”</p><p>Part of the revenue piece is the eventual size of the playoff, which the Big Ten wants to see go from 12 teams to 24. More CFP games would mean more money. But some of that would just cancel out what the Big Ten would lose by killing its championship game — which almost certainly would happen with an expanded playoff, Pettiti said.</p><p>The spiraling costs of staying competitive in college sports and what role the federal government might have in regulating it are new — and urgent — topics.</p><p>But fans can be forgiven for wanting to return to the days when the biggest question was which conference was king.</p>

entries.title: White Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami's hometown struck by 7.1 magnitude earthquake
entries.summary: <p>White Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami’s hometown of Kumamoto, Japan, was hit by a 7.1 magnitude earthquake Tuesday that reportedly has killed at least 13 people and left many missing.</p><p>“I was really surprised and devastated by the news,” Murakami said through translate Kenzo Yagi. “The last earthquake I experienced was 10 years back. Obviously, it’s really hard to swallow. I was deeply in shock.”</p><p>Murakami said the area was just beginning to recover fully from the earthquake in 2016 that killed at least 50 people. He learned of the recent earthquake Tuesday morning and said he was able to contact all of his relatives, who are safe.</p><p>His parents, who threw out ceremonial first pitches Sunday at Rate Field, had planned to stay in Chicago through the Sox’ homestand but headed home Tuesday instead. Their home in the city, where Murakami was born, is fine. He was in high school when the last earthquake struck.</p><p>“It’s not like it flashes back,” he said. “It’s more the overall concern about the people and everybody who is affected by the disaster.”</p><p>Murakami said he hopes playing for the Sox can help keep people’s spirits up in his hometown.</p><p>“I always get a lot of cheers from everybody back in Japan, and that’s what gives me power to play baseball,” he said. “As a professional baseball player, I would like to give back by playing hard and something to cheer on for the people back in Kumamoto.”</p><p>Bullet train services and some airport operations remained suspended, and damage was still being assessed on the southern main island of Kyushu.</p><p>About 36,900 homes were still without electricity, 9,500 homes were without gas and communication networks were not working in some areas, chief government spokesman Minoru Kihara told reporters.</p><p><i>The Associated Press contributed to this report.</i></p>

entries.title: It's all hands on deck in White Sox' bullpen — all game, every game
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox’ bullpen is like the weather in Chicago: You never know what you’re going to get.</p><p>Neither do the relievers, for that matter.</p><p>Take left-hander Bryan Hudson, for example. Last Wednesday, he closed out a two-run victory against the Rangers with a perfect ninth inning that included two strikeouts. Two days later, he entered in the sixth inning with a four-run lead, the bases loaded and no outs. He allowed four runs in two-thirds of an inning and took the loss.</p><p>Is that indicative of ineffective usage? Do relievers need defined roles to succeed?</p><p>That’s what many teams prefer, but manager Will Venable and the Sox seem to prefer giving relievers defined situations, whenever they occur in a game. And given the starters’ inability to pitch deep into games, relievers have pitched in more situations than the Sox would like.</p><p>That continued Tuesday, with left-hander Anthony Kay lasting 5 ⅓ innings in a 3-2 loss to the Yankees. In the Sox’ last 24 games, only Sean Burke has thrown at least six innings, which he has done four times. The other four-fifths of the rotation keeps putting the bullpen in precarious positions.</p><p>Perhaps that’s why Venable uses his bullpen the way he does. Hudson said that’s unique.</p><p>“I think every team has their own unique way of using the bullpen,” he told the Sun-Times. “We’ve got a younger team with not necessarily defined roles whatsoever. Other teams in the past, they’ve had a defined closer or whatnot.</p><p>“But with us being a younger squad, I think the all-hands-on-deck thing keeps us all locked in and ready to go. It gives anybody and everybody that equal opportunity to go out there and prove themselves any given night.”</p><p>That it does, but it also doesn’t allow for much predictability, which can affect a player’s routine. Still, it has worked for the Sox more times than it hasn’t.</p><p>“There’s not a right or a wrong way,” right-handed reliever Trevor Richards told the Sun-Times. “A lot of it depends on the people you have because it’s a different mentality, especially if you’re not sure what’s going to happen that day.</p><p>“I would say half of our bullpen is locked in from [inning] one through nine. You’re ready to go all game long, which takes its toll over the course of the year, but you also get used to it and change how you get ready. I think most of our guys handle it well.”</p><p>Richards certainly does. Since the All-Star break, he has entered games anywhere from the fourth to ninth inning. He has pitched in high- and low-leverage situations and has gotten anywhere from one out to six. He entered Tuesday having thrown two innings in three of the previous four days.</p><p>“He just always wants to pitch. He’s incredible,” Venable said. “He makes himself available every single day. Really have to be proactive in protecting him because he will say that he is available to pitch every single day. He’s been awesome.”</p><p>Venable likely would say the same about lefty Sean Newcomb, who also has been called on to pitch multiple innings multiple times. In fact, he’s one of six Sox relievers to start and finish a game this season. Fireballing righty Grant Taylor is another, and he has many outings with multiple innings, as well. If you’re pitching out of the Sox’ pen, expect to do a little of everything.</p><p>“Our job down in the bullpen is to be ready to come in whenever they call our names,” Hudson said. “There’s no real roles down in the bullpen. We’re all hands on deck. In some sense, we’re like firemen. You got to come in and put out the fire.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.summary: <p>After winning home games at a 66% clip before the All-Star break, the White Sox suddenly are finding Rate Field to be a tougher place to play.</p><p>With their 3-2 loss to the Yankees on Tuesday, the Sox fell to 1-4 on their first homestand after the break. Maybe it’s the law of averages taking hold. Or maybe it’s the quality of the opponents. Either way, it doesn’t bode well for the Sox, who are in the midst of a 13-game stretch against teams currently in playoff position.</p><p>“I think it just kind of unfolds that way,” Sox manager Will Venable said of his team’s home rut. “There’s not one thing that we can point to in our preparation or how we’re going about things any differently at home or on the road. Sometimes it’s just how the chips fall.</p><p>“This stretch here at home just hasn’t been as clean and as good as we have hoped for, but got an opportunity tomorrow.”</p><p>The Sox had one opportunity to score against veteran right-hander Gerrit Cole and couldn’t cash in. Munetaka Murakami doubled to lead off the fourth, and Miguel Vargas followed with a walk. After Colson Montgomery flied out, Andrew Benintendi advanced the runners with a groundout. Braden Montgomery walked to load the bases, but Tristan Peters popped out.</p><p>“He was really good,” Venable said of Cole, who allowed two walks and four hits and struck out seven in six scoreless innings. “Established the fastball, which we expected him to do. Really good slider. Traffic there in the fourth, but couldn’t push anything across.”</p><p>The Yankees pushed three across against Sox left-hander Anthony Kay in the second, and that proved to be just enough. After striking out the side for the first time in his major-league career in the first inning, Kay allowed two singles to start the second. Both advanced on a wild pitch.</p><p>Anthony Volpe followed with a double off the wall in center field, but only one runner scored because Peters had a chance to catch it. One out later, Max Schuemann took advantage of the infield playing in by chopping one over Vargas’ head at third, scoring two runs.</p><p>Venable defended playing the infield in so early in the game.</p><p>“We don’t want them to score anymore,” he said. “That’s the play for us. That’s something that we’ve been aggressive with all year. Obviously, when it doesn’t work out, you stand up here and explain why. But it was the right time to do it. Just one of those moves that doesn’t work out.”</p><p>Otherwise, Kay was sharp. He allowed three runs, five hits and one walk and struck out seven.</p><p>“It was really good,” he said. “Other than that second inning, it was probably the best command I’ve had all year. [The ball] just feels smooth coming out of my hand. Overall, it’s just been better.</p><p>“We’re trying to be a little bit more explosive on the leg kick. I feel like in the past, it’s just been a little, not lazy, just a little slow from the top. And now we’re working on being a little bit more explosive out of the top and trying to get down the mound a little bit faster.”</p><p>The Sox finally got on the board in the ninth against closer David Bednar. Rookie Braden Montgomery, the only Sox player with two hits in the game, singled and scored on Chase Meidroth’s two-out homer. But pinch hitter Everson Pereira struck out to end it.</p><p>Now the Sox will look to salvage a split with the Yankees after dropping a sloppy game Monday and a tough one Tuesday — before things get even tougher with road series against the American League-leading Rays and the resurgent Red Sox.</p><p>“The main point right now is defensively to clean some things up, baserunning-wise clean some things up, which I thought we did a good job of today,” Venable said. “Got to keep moving forward, find ways to score against some really good pitchers.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module entries.title: Illinois stacks the deck against independent candidates
entries.summary: <p>Last week, the Sun-Times reported on an egregious abuse in our election system in a story headlined online "<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/21/byron-sigcho-lopez-mayra-macias-chuy-garcia-congressional-seat-independent-candidates-ballot-removal" >Sigcho-Lopez, Macías won’t appear on November ballot for Rep. García’s seat, state board rules</a>."</p><p>"In Illinois, independents running for congressional seats must submit a minimum of 10,816 petition signatures, compared to just 697 for Democrats and 371 for Republicans," Tina Sfondeles reported. </p><p>There are all kinds of problems here, including the problem that very few seem to think there are any problems at all. And nothing will change unless and until somebody keeps shedding light on these following problems, and the people who can fix them take action:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-33baf3a1-86c7-11f1-bda1-f57b829e9a15" start="1"><li> There is no reason for the disparity in the number of signatures needed to get on the ballot. It is simply unfair and unjust.<br></li><li> Requiring a candidate to get signatures gives an edge to candidates of major political parties, who have more money and workers. We need independent candidates to shake things up a bit. Too many votes are along party lines.<br></li><li>Petition signatures are meaningless in the first place unless they represent people who actually endorse the candidate. Many people are not signing petitions to show support for a candidate.<br></li><li>The only qualification for running for office is filling out paperwork and then spending a ridiculous amount of time and money on getting signatures on a petition.<br></li><li>These petitions often result in legal challenges that require everybody involved to hire legal counsel. So we then need candidates of financial means who can afford this.</li></ol><p>We are severely limiting our candidate pool unnecessarily and unwisely.</p><p>Who makes up these rules? Nobody has to demonstrate any competence or ability to become a candidate, but they must have this ability to get strangers to sign this paper.</p><p>I say, anybody who wants to run for Congress, give them three hours and a computer. Give them a list of problems in our state and our nation, and let them tell us what they would do about them. The would-be candidate can include their own list too. The would-be candidate can also include any relevant information on why they should be in Congress.</p><p>Their answers would be anonymous until people have had the opportunity to read and discuss the answers. The party leaders can choose however many candidates they want out of these. Independents can have their papers posted on a website, and the public can select viable options.</p><p>This is far better than the way we choose candidates today. We can and need to do better than what we are doing now.</p><p><i>Larry Craig, Wilmette</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9a0000" name="module-9a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Protect vulnerable Chicagoans from wildfire smoke </h3><p>Wildfire smoke recently pushed Chicago’s air quality into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-prompts-air-quality-alert-for-most-of-chicago-area-to" target="_blank" >hazardous ranges</a>, raising urgent questions about whether the city is prepared to protect residents.</p><p>Severe smoke exposure is a public health emergency. It can <a class="Link" href="https://www.epa.gov/wildfire-smoke-course/health-effects-attributed-wildfire-smoke-0" target="_blank" >worsen pulmonary and cardiovascular health, increase susceptibility to infections and even result in premature death</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1352231026000026" target="_blank" >A study of Chicago’s 2023 wildfire smoke episode</a> found that the smoke increased ground-level ozone, a lung irritant that can aggravate asthma and other preexisting chronic illnesses. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.10.079" target="_blank" >A study following the 2025 Los Angeles fires</a> found an increase in emergency room visits for respiratory problems, heart attacks and other health issues over the next three months.</p><p>Although the dangers of wildfire smoke extend across Chicago, residents do not have equal means to protect themselves. Low-income families may lack effective air filtration, be unable to avoid outdoor work and might face greater barriers to obtaining timely medical care when symptoms develop. </p><p>Through my research at New Life Volunteering Society, a Chicago-based free clinic primarily serving uninsured patients, I have come to understand how barriers to healthcare can cause manageable and preventable conditions to become life-threatening.</p><p>Chicago public health officials should boost screenings and health education programs, especially for residents with asthma, emphysema and other preexisting respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. Such programs — if they aren't already — should connect residents with timely medical care, provide N95 masks and other necessary supplies, and issue clear guidance on reducing smoke exposure and recognizing when symptoms require medical attention. </p><p>All future efforts should be developed with free clinics and community health centers, which already understand and serve the needs of disadvantaged communities.</p><p>As wildfire smoke poses a growing threat, we need leaders to keep expanding a coordinated response that protects the health of all Chicago residents.</p><p><i>Jay Dalal, Northwestern University student</i></p><h3>New Ryan Field is more about VIP glitz than football </h3><p>So the Sun-Times' Ben Pope thinks Northwestern’s old Ryan Field was "a dump" (<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/07/21/northwestern-football-new-ryan-field-stadium-review" >Ryan Remade Right, July 22</a>). I beg to differ. Of course, my interest was watching college football, something that no longer exists in our time of the annual renting of players and games played mainly for TV ratings.</p><p>Does it make sense that Northwestern built a stadium matched to today’s product? I wonder if Mr. Pope saw what rests in the vast spaces behind those 35,000 seats: expansive club amenities that cater to fans willing to pay big money to access them. Elite private spaces and experiences <a class="Link" href="https://www.newryanfield.com/reimagined/premium-exp" target="_blank" >described by Northwestern</a> as “designed to rival Chicago’s finest restaurants.” There's "a hidden garden entrance, beautiful patio, refined interiors.” Another offers “a country club experience."</p><p>If you visit this grand 'cat palace with no interest in watching the game, you’ll surely have a luxurious good time. However, if you feel that what college football has become — what Northwestern is now trying to cash in on — no longer aligns with your values, then it's time to, ahem, dump this New Ryan Field.</p><p><i>Clark McCain, Ravenswood</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Woman stuck in a rut after move to new area
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have been married 45 years, but over the last six months, we've had numerous fights about Facebook. I'm having issues with his addiction to social media and his constant posts and comments with people I don't know.</p><p>I get jealous about these interactions with women. He has never given me reason not to trust him, but I'm having trouble with this. It's also a problem when he has one or two alcoholic drinks. If I ask him about something FB-related, it sometimes sets him off and we have a big fight. He becomes very unreasonable, and it's always my fault. In person, he's very friendly and sometimes teases women. I get jealous about that, too.</p><p>We recently moved to this area and don't have many friends, and that seems to be making things worse. I'm feeling sad and lack self-esteem right now. I don't know how to get over this. Do you have any suggestions? He won't go to counseling because he says it's "my problem," not his. — <i>ALWAYS WRONG IN WEST VIRGINIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR ALWAYS WRONG:</b> Your husband appears to be a "people person." Nowhere in your letter did you indicate that he has been unfaithful. It would be wrong to try to change his personality because you feel insecure.</p><p>A way for you (both) to make friends in a new community would be to involve yourselves in it. Join a club or a service organization, sign up for a gym or volunteer to help others who are less fortunate. If you and your husband are religious, affiliate with a house of worship. This should facilitate integrating yourselves. However, if your sadness and lack of self-esteem don't lessen, then discuss this with a licensed mental health professional.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My daughter, "Amelia," is 26 and has been dating her boyfriend for almost three years. He is great, and my family loves him. He has a son from a previous relationship who was born while my daughter was dating him. (He and the baby's mom broke up while she was pregnant.) Amelia is great with the little boy, but we want more for her. We would love to see the relationship go further, but although he keeps telling her it's going to happen "soon," it never does.</p><p>Amelia has taken on many roles, and I believe she deserves more of a commitment from him. She helps to raise his son with nothing in return but empty promises. Are my husband and I wrong for wanting more for her? She has expressed that she also wants the commitment. Should we approach the subject with him? — <i>MAMA WANTS MORE</i></p><p><b>DEAR MAMA:</b> I don't think it would be wise for you and your husband to approach Amelia's boyfriend and try to wrest a commitment from him. You do, however, need to air your feelings with your daughter. She could remain in limbo for years if she doesn't assert herself. If the romance doesn't work out, the person who may suffer most is that little boy, who will have lost another mother figure.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>Good advice for everyone — teens to seniors — is in "The Anger in All of Us and How to Deal With It." To order, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Anger Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: ComEd's $15 billion grid plan fuels questionable spending
entries.summary: <p>As Illinois families brace for another season of high energy bills, ComEd’s parent company, Exelon, has been working hard to convince the public it is standing up for customers. </p><p>In February, Exelon <a class="Link" href="https://www.exeloncorp.com/newsroom/exelon-launches-the-exelon-promise-to-fight-out-of-control-energy-costs" target="_blank" >launched</a> “The Exelon Promise,” pledging to protect customers “regardless of market conditions” and ensure large energy users like data centers “pay their fair share of the grid investments needed to support them," in the words of CEO Calvin Butler.</p><p>ComEd’s own filings before the Illinois Commerce Commission tell a different story.</p><p>Expert testimony <a class="Link" href="https://www.citizensutilityboard.org/blog/2026/06/29/cub-testimony-uncovers-1-billion-in-questionable-comed-spending/" target="_blank" >filed</a> by the Citizens Utility Board in the case over ComEd’s proposed $15.3 billion, four-year grid plan has identified more than $1 billion in spending that CUB says is inflated, unjustified or mislabeled to dodge legal scrutiny.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4e0000" name="module-4e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>That should concern every Illinois customer. This is on top of a plan that already represents a 21% spending increase over ComEd’s last one, a plan the Illinois Commerce Commission <a class="Link" href="https://www.citizensutilityboard.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/20241219_ComEdFinalOrder.pdf" target="_blank" >rejected</a> outright in 2023 for failing to prove it was affordable.</p><p>CUB’s expert testimony points to a familiar pattern for ComEd: It chooses higher-cost utility spending over lower-cost customer protection. CUB says ComEd overstated summer peak-demand investments by about $238 million, largely by skipping lower-cost options like demand-response programs in favor of an overall budget hike. </p><p>The utility also wants to spend $209.4 million replacing smart meters that are still operational and haven’t even been fully paid off yet. Customers would ultimately cover those replacement costs through higher bills. To top it off, ComEd wants to do it without competitive bidding and without guaranteeing customers real-time access to their own usage data. </p><p>Then there are electric vehicles. ComEd inflated its EV-charging cost estimates by $124 million, CUB said, by assuming worst-case scenarios that don’t hold up, like counting on electric school buses to strain the summer grid, when school isn’t even in session.</p><p>The most troubling finding is not just how much ComEd wants to spend, but how it is trying to classify the spending. CUB identified $96 million in capital spending, plus $18 million more in operating costs, that ComEd labeled “mandatory” even though it’s clearly discretionary. That distinction matters under the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, known as CEJA. CUB found that "ComEd hid these expenses in the mandatory category to skirt the CEJA mandate of having to prove that the benefits of discretionary spending outweigh the costs."</p><p>Regulators already flagged this exact move in ComEd’s last plan, when 72% of proposed spending was declared "mandatory.” ComEd’s response wasn’t to fix it. The new plan pushes that figure to 75%.</p><p>This is typical behavior for monopoly utilities like ComEd. Consumer advocates cut $2 billion, about a quarter, from ComEd’s last grid plan before the Illinois Commerce Commission would approve it. Once again, it’s outside experts who are catching more than a billion dollars in questionable costs headed for Illinois customers.</p><p>That’s the gap Exelon needs to close. A company cannot promise to protect customers “regardless of market conditions” while seeking approval of a grid plan filled with premature equipment swaps, capacity built on unverified projections and spending mislabeled to sidestep a state law designed to protect ratepayers.</p><p>The Illinois Commerce Commission is expected to issue a proposed order in October and a final order by the end of the year. That gives ComEd time to bring its filing in line with what Exelon promised the public in February: making data centers put real money down before they plug in, and an end to disguising discretionary spending as mandatory. </p><p>Exelon made a public promise to Illinois ratepayers. Now, they have a duty to ensure ComEd keeps it, in a case that will decide how high their bills are set to soar.</p><p><i>State Rep. Angie Guerrero-Cuellar, D-Chicago, represents the 22nd Illinois House District. </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f50000" name="module-f50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.summary: <p>A tale of abuse, mental illness and death, Lady in Red’s monologue is the most harrowing in “For Colored Girls Who Have Considered Suicide / When the Rainbow Is Enuf.”</p><p>But actress Teena Marie is embracing the role with confidence and conviction.</p><p>“I can visualize it because I’ve been there, and I’ve seen it,” said Marie, who stars in ETA Creative Arts Foundation’s upcoming rendition of the late Ntozake Shange’s landmark 1976 play. Directed by Donn Carl Harper, the production opens Saturday and runs through Aug. 30 at the group’s Grand Crossing theater.</p><p>“I have family that went through mental health issues. I’ve witnessed aunties putting the man before the kids until it was too late.”</p><p>Beyond nailing the part, Marie said she is driven by a mission to help women leave dangerous second play written by a Black woman to be performed on Broadway. entries.title: A Rohingya Muslim immigrant dreamed of opening a restaurant. Now she owns Asian Homecook in West Ridge
entries.summary: <p>Toyuba Amir Ali would prepare large meals for family and friends in her West Ridge home, with dishes like <i>mee goreng mamak ayam, </i>a stir-fried noodle dish tossed in a sweet and spicy sambal chile-based sauce and protein and <i>nasi goreng kampung</i>, a salty and spicy dish made of day-old rice, anchovies, shrimp paste and topped with a fried egg.</p><p>She worked as a cook at a restaurant in Malaysia and at one point owned a food stall with a friend. When the Rohingya Muslim immigrant came to the U.S. in September 2024, she began dreaming of opening her own eatery. But her daughter Aishah Hamid and her siblings weren’t crazy about the idea. However, when it became clear that Amir Ali wasn’t going to let the dream go, Hamid and various family members mobilized to support the matriarch’s vision.</p><p>“She came up with the idea to open a restaurant and kept saying, ‘maybe we should try,’” said Hamid, 35. “But we weren’t familiar with opening or running a restaurant. However, she kept saying ‘the restaurant is calling me.’ We were not her biggest supporters. I kept saying ‘let’s not do it. It’s too much of a hassle.’ But she really wanted to so we ended up helping her anyway.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Kampung</h3><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p>2 tablespoons oil<br>A handful of dried anchovies (ikan bilis)<br>4 shallots, roughly chopped<br>2 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed<br>3 bird’s eye chiles, roughly chopped<br>1 tablespoon toasted belacan (shrimp paste)<br>A handful of kangkung (water spinach)<br>3 cups cooked cold rice<br>1 tablespoon oyster sauce<br>1 fried egg<br>Sliced cucumbers</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Heat oil in a pan and fry the anchovies until crispy. Remove and set aside.</p><p>In a mortar and pestle, combine the shallots, garlic cloves and chiles to create a paste. </p><p>In the same pan you fried the anchovies, add the blended shallots, garlic, chiles and toasted belacan until fragrant. Add kangkung and cook briefly until wilted.</p><p>Add the rice and oyster sauce. Stir-fry until everything is well combined. Mix in some of the anchovies and top with the remaining crispy anchovies before serving. To serve, add a fried egg and sliced cucumbers on the side.</p>

entries.title: 'Like getting paid to party': The life of cover bands on the Chicago festival circuit
entries.summary: <p>It’s a nearly perfect Sunday afternoon in Chicago: sunny, 75 degrees, albeit with a little wildfire smoke. Chrissie Olstad brushes back her burgundy hair. She’s got her boots and fishnet tights on. She’s ready to jump onstage at a festival on the city’s North Side.</p><p>“I am so excited,” Olstad said. “We love the Burger Fest in Roscoe Village. We're gonna rock it out.”</p><p>It’s the height of summer in Chicago and no matter where you go, a street festival is likely just around the corner. Restaurateurs are serving popular bites, makers and artisans are selling handmade goods and in the air is the sound of Fleetwood Mac — but that’s not Stevie Nicks singing.</p><p>Cover and tribute bands are street fest staples. The musicians aren’t performing their own original pieces but music that a general crowd will bop along to because it’s familiar. Olstad is the lead singer and rhythm guitarist of The Gingers; everyone in the band has red hair, mostly artificial.</p><p>“It’s kind of crazy, but fun, thrilling, yet scary at times. But overall, very enjoyable,” Olstad said about life as a Chicago cover band musician.</p><p>The Gingers have an eclectic catalog: They’ll play classics from Led Zeppelin and Heart to more contemporary tunes. Kerri Jane, the band’s bassist, said the music they play has true emotional meaning.</p><p>“It takes [people] back in time to times in their life when things are a little less stressful, maybe a little happier,” she said. “So we help bring back some emotional healing.” These bands are bringing nostalgia to the neighborhoods, but just because they aren’t playing original music doesn’t mean it isn’t a lot of work. Curious City spoke with three bands that are regulars on the local festival circuit to get a peek behind the scenes.</p><h3>The Gingers</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div From left to right: lead guitarist Debbie Cielen, drummer Liz Ele, lead vocalist Chrissie Olstad, keyboardist Emi Fukuda, and bassist Kerri Jane.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Before creating The Gingers in 2015, co-founders Chrissie Olstad and Debbie Cielen played original music in their band Hag. “That really didn't go over too well,” Olstad said. “I mean, it was a joke, but it was like, ‘OK, we got some fresh blood in the band.’ So ‘The Gingers,’ that was perfect.” Olstad and Cielen decided to add younger musicians to the lineup and play covers only. On performance day, all the band members sport some form of “luxurious red hair,” whether it’s dyed or a wig.</p><p><b>Members: </b>Chrissie Olstad, guitar and vocals; Debbie Cielen, vocals and lead and slide guitar; Kerri Jane, bass and vocals; Emi Fukuda, keyboard, guitar and flute; Liz Ele, drums.</p><p><b>Where to see them: </b>Festivals and bars in Chicago and the suburbs <a class="Link" A few members are LGBTQ+, and the band’s busiest time is Pride Month in June.</p><p><b>Members:</b> Molly Callinan, lead vocals; Nicholas Ray, lead vocals; Vinnie VanAction, guitar; Maddi Vogel, drums; Alex Newkirk, keyboard; Lunchbreak, bass.</p><p>Like many cover bands, Too Much Molly’s members all hold additional jobs, from retail positions to nonprofits supporting Chinese adoptees. Vinnie Van Action works as a classroom assistant in special education schools, so when summer break hits, he’s free to dedicate more time to the band. I just find my wildest outfit. From left, singer and guitarist Justin Horvath-Adair, backing vocalist Elya Bottiger, lead singer Amanda Horvath-Adair, drummer Keith Daproza, lead singer Cheryl Jennison Daproza, bass player Davide Pezzini, and pianist Micky York.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Steve Jurkovic/Provided by Amanda Horvath-Adair.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dancing Queen: An ABBA Salute started in 2004. Tribute bands typically cover one band or artist. Dancing Queen used to be called ABBA Salute, but the original Swedish quartet has a strong legal team which prohibits tribute bands from using “ABBA” in the main portion of its name. Dancing Queen is something close to local celebrities, and some shows book more than a year in advance.</p><p><b>Members:</b> Micky York as Benny Andersson on vocals, keyboard and accordion; Amanda Horvath-Adair as Agnetha Fältskog on vocals; Justin Horvath-Adair as Björn Ulvaeus on vocals; Cheryl Jennison Daproza as Anni-Frid Lyngstad on vocals; Davide Pezzini on bass; Keith Daproza on drums</p><p>Behind the scenes, members of Dancing Queen double as the band’s social media marketer, website administrator, costume designer and business manager.
